client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away a few months ago. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of something and just completely lose track of what I was doing, and then I feel this wave of sadness or sometimes this anger that I don't even fully understand. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're experiencing — the scattered focus, the waves of sadness, even that confusing anger — are all very natural responses to losing someone so important to you. Grief doesn't follow a neat path, and it makes complete sense that it's spilling into every corner of your life right now. You mentioned you're not sure talking will change anything, which is a honest and understandable feeling to have — can you tell me a little more about what "change" would look like for you, or what you're hoping might feel different?

client: Honestly, I think what I want most is just to be able to get through a workday without falling apart, or at least without feeling like I'm completely useless. Like, I used to be someone who could stay on top of things, and now I can't even finish a simple email without my mind drifting to my dad and then feeling this guilt that I'm even trying to work instead of... I don't know, grieving properly or something. I guess I'm not even sure what "better" looks like anymore, which is part of what scares me.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — feeling like focusing on work somehow means you're not grieving "right" — is such a common but painful trap, and I want to gently challenge the idea that there's a "proper" way to grieve at all. The fact that you *can* still show up and try to work isn't a betrayal of your dad; it's actually a sign of your resilience, even when it doesn't feel that way. I'm curious — when that guilt shows up and tells you you're doing grief "wrong," whose voice does it sound like, or where do you think that belief comes from?

client: That's a hard question, honestly. I think part of it might be my dad himself — he was someone who wore his emotions openly, and he always said our family didn't run away from hard feelings, so there's this voice in my head that says pushing through work is somehow running away. But then I also wonder if I'm just making excuses to feel bad, which I know sounds strange, and I'm not sure I fully buy the idea that going to work is "resilience" — it kind of just feels like I'm avoiding sitting with the grief because sitting with it is unbearable.
therapist: It doesn't sound strange at all — you're holding two really painful thoughts at once: that working means you're running away, and that maybe you're somehow choosing to feel bad, and both of those are worth examining gently. I also want to reflect something back to you: you just described sitting with grief as "unbearable," which tells me you *have* sat with it, at least enough to know how heavy it is — that's not avoidance, that's someone who's been in real pain. I wonder, when you imagine what your dad meant by "not running away from hard feelings," do you think he would have seen you trying to survive your days as running away — or might he have understood it differently?

client: When you put it that way, I want to say he would have understood, but I honestly don't know — and that uncertainty is its own kind of painful, because I can't ask him anymore. There's this part of me that wants to believe he'd say "you're doing what you need to do," but then another part worries I'm just reshaping his memory to make myself feel better, which feels like another kind of betrayal. I think that's what makes this so hard to untangle, because I keep second-guessing even the comfort I try to give myself.
therapist: What you're describing — distrusting your own comfort — is one of grief's cruelest tricks, turning even the small moments of relief into new sources of guilt. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: remembering your dad in a way that feels kind and understanding isn't reshaping his memory, it's actually an act of love, and it makes sense that your mind reaches for the version of him that felt safe. I'm wondering — in the moments when you do let yourself believe he'd understand, even briefly, what does that feel like in your body, and does it feel like betrayal, or something else?

client: When I let myself go there, even for a second, it actually feels like... relief, I guess, almost like exhaling after holding your breath for too long. But it doesn't last, because almost immediately I notice I feel relieved and then I tense up again, like I'm not allowed to have that. I hear what you're saying about it being an act of love, but I'm not sure I can just decide to believe that — it feels like something that would need to be true before I could feel it, not something I can think my way into.
therapist: That exhale you described is really important — your body and heart already know how to find some peace, even if your mind rushes in to take it away, and that relief isn't a mistake or a weakness, it's a glimpse of what's possible. You're also making a really wise point that you can't just *decide* to believe something — beliefs shift through experience, not just logic, which is actually very much how I'd want to work with you rather than just talking you into a new perspective. So I'm curious — what if we treated that brief moment of relief not as something you have to earn or justify, but as a small piece of evidence worth paying attention to: what would it mean if that exhale was telling you something true?

client: I think if that exhale was telling me something true, it might mean that my dad actually would have been okay with me surviving this, which is both comforting and somehow makes me want to cry right now. But I'm a little wary of building too much on one fleeting feeling — like, what if I'm just grasping at something because I want it to be true, not because it actually is? I guess I'm not sure how you're supposed to tell the difference between a moment of genuine insight and just wishful thinking.
therapist: The fact that it made you want to cry feels significant to me — wishful thinking tends to feel like relief without weight, but what you just touched seems to carry both comfort *and* grief at the same time, which is often closer to truth than to fantasy. You're right to hold it carefully rather than grasp at it, and I don't think you have to decide right now whether it's insight or wishful thinking — both can coexist, and the question itself shows how deeply you loved him. I'm wondering, over the coming days, if you notice that exhale feeling again — even briefly — would you be open to just observing it without immediately putting it on trial, and seeing what it does or doesn't tell you?

client: I think I can try that, but I'm a little worried that "just observing" is easier said than done — my mind doesn't really have a neutral gear, it tends to immediately start analyzing and judging whatever I'm feeling. And honestly, part of me wonders if noticing those moments will just make me more aware of how quickly they disappear, which might end up feeling worse. But I don't know, maybe that's my skepticism talking, and it does seem like a smaller ask than trying to change what I believe.
therapist: Your mind's tendency to immediately analyze isn't a flaw — it's actually been a useful tool for you, and we're not trying to switch it off, just gently slow it down by even a second or two before the judging kicks in. Your concern about noticing how quickly the relief disappears is really valid, and it's worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as just skepticism — but I'd also offer that even a moment you can *name* is a moment you had, and that's different from it never happening at all. What if, instead of trying to hold onto those moments, you just gave yourself permission to briefly acknowledge them — even something as simple as a quiet "there it was" — and we see together what that's like?

client: "There it was" — that's actually a phrase I think I could manage, it feels small enough that it doesn't demand anything from me. I guess my hesitation is that it still feels a little like I'm doing an exercise, and I don't want my grief to become a project I'm managing, if that makes sense. But maybe that's not what you're suggesting, and I think I'm willing to at least notice if it happens this week without immediately tearing it apart.
therapist: What you just named - not wanting grief to become a project - is something I want to hold onto, because it tells me something important about what you need this to feel like, and I don't want to lose that. "There it was" isn't really an exercise so much as a tiny act of witnessing yourself, the same way your dad might have — just acknowledging that something real happened, without needing to do anything with it. As you move through this week, I'm curious whether there's a difference for you between *managing* grief and simply *being* with it, even imperfectly?

client: I think there is a difference, but I'm struggling to articulate it — managing feels like I'm standing outside the grief with a clipboard, and being with it feels more like just... sitting in the same room as it, which honestly sounds terrifying. I'm not sure I know how to do the second one without either shutting down completely or getting swept away by it. But something about the way you framed "witnessing yourself the way your dad might have" actually landed differently for me, and I want to sit with that for a bit.
therapist: That image of sitting in the same room as grief — rather than managing it from a distance — is really beautiful and honest, and the fact that it feels terrifying makes complete sense, because you've already felt how much is in that room. I'm glad the idea of witnessing yourself the way your dad might have landed for you, and I want you to know you don't have to figure out how to "be with it" all at once — even just holding that image gently this week is enough. When you imagine your dad sitting in that room with you, not fixing anything, just present — what does that feel like?

client: When I imagine that, I actually feel something loosen a little in my chest, like the room isn't quite as unbearable if he's in it too. But then there's this immediate sadness because it's not real — he's not actually here, and imagining him there almost makes the absence feel sharper somehow. I don't know if that means the image is helpful or if I'm just finding new ways to hurt myself with it.
therapist: That loosening in your chest is real, even if the image is imagined — your nervous system responded to something true about how safe your dad made you feel, and that safety lives in you because he put it there. The sharpness of his absence that follows isn't the image hurting you; it's love with nowhere to go right now, which is one of the most painful parts of grief. I wonder if both things can be true at once — that imagining him there brings some comfort *and* reminds you of the loss — and that sitting with that contradiction, rather than deciding the image is helpful or harmful, might be exactly what "being in the room" with grief looks like?
